---
title: "Europeanisation and the economy"
subtitle: "Economic crisis and EU framing in the Eurobarometer, 2004–2013"
bibliography: [references.bib, references-new.bib]
---



The case study presented on this site is built on a single claim from a paper, published by the original author in the *European Sociological Review* [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], on how citizens of the European Union understood the EU during the economic crisis. The claim went through every kind of check that the SCORE programme applied to published research, among them a reanalysis by five independent analysts in the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], one of whom, analyst C6HJR, is the facilitator of this course. The boxes that open on a click contain evidence that a reader may wish to verify, although the argument can be followed without them.

## 1. The original study {#sec-study}

### 1.1 Questions and hypotheses {#sec-questions}

The paper starts from a distinction between the affective component of attitudes towards the EU, such as a sense of belonging to Europe, and their cognitive component, the meanings that citizens attach to the EU, which in the view of the original author had "received much less attention so far" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 620]. The stated aim of the paper is to investigate "the effect of the current economic crisis, the resulting EU financial stability support program, and the politicization of the EU on subjective Europeanization", and thereby to "assess the dynamics of EU attitudes among citizens from the 27 EU member states between 2004 and 2013" (p. 620). The author refers to these meanings as 'EU framing' and distinguishes four dimensions of it, obtained by crossing the valence of a meaning, positive or negative, with its content, materialist or not.

|   | Materialist | Non-materialist |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------------|
| Positive | **Utilitarian**: "the EU framed in material advantages such as economic prosperity and social protection" | **Cosmopolitan**: "the EU framed as a cosmopolitan legal order that includes terms such as peace, democracy and cultural diversity" |
| Negative | **Libertarian**: "the EU considered as a bureaucratic waste of money" | **Communitarian**: "the EU perceived as a threat to the own constitutive community" |

: The four dimensions of EU framing, in the words of the paper (p. 620).

The paper derives five hypotheses in its theoretical sections, two of which have two parts, and the three examined in the course read as follows.

- "H1: Poor national economic performances significantly increase the negative and decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. The effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions of EU framing." (p. 621)
- "H2a: High-educated citizens endorse positive dimensions to a larger extent and negative dimensions of EU framing to a lower extent than low-educated citizens." (p. 621)
- "H2b: High-educated citizens are more strongly affected by an economic downturn than low-educated citizens in their endorsement of EU framing. The magnitude of the interaction term between educational level and economic performance is larger for the materialist dimensions of EU framing." (p. 621)

The remaining hypotheses, H3 to H5b (p. 622), concern the net fiscal transfer of a country to the EU budget, its receipt of EU financial stability support, and the support for European integration among its political parties together with the salience of the EU issue among those parties, all of which lie outside the claim under test.

It was the first hypothesis that the reanalyses tested, and the abstract reports the corresponding finding in the sentence from which the claim was later extracted: "The results show, first, that poor economic performances increase negative and decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (p. 619). The reasoning behind the hypothesis follows what the paper calls the 'sociotropic perspective', in which citizens judge the EU by the performance of their national economy rather than by their own circumstances (p. 620). The original author expected the crisis to matter more than the gentler economic fluctuations examined in earlier studies, since "citizens' EU attitudes are much more likely to be strongly affected by an abrupt and lasting economic recession than by smooth and small changes in economic performance over time" (p. 621).

### 1.2 The Standard Eurobarometer {#sec-eurobarometer}

The data come from the Standard Eurobarometer, a repeated survey of the populations in the EU member states, conducted on behalf of the European Commission under the responsibility of its Directorate-General for Communication and documented for re-use, wave by wave, by the GESIS Data Archive for the Social Sciences. Each wave draws "multistage random probability samples for each EU member state" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 622], with a target of about 1,000 completed interviews in each country (variable report for the wave of spring 2004, GESIS study ZA4056, p. VII).

The wave of spring 2004, which predates the accession of the ten new member states, interviewed 16,216 people in the fifteen states of the time, while each of the later waves comprises between about 26,600 and 26,900 respondents in the twenty-seven states covered by the paper.

Two features of the survey limit the analyses that it can support. GESIS supplies a post-stratification weight, which adjusts each national sample to the population by sex, age, region and size of locality, but "A design weight which would adjust for unequal selection probabilities (depending on the household size) is not made available" (p. VIII). And, as the original author notes, "detailed information on the response rates for each EB wave is not publicly available, which hampers the assessment of survey data quality" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. Since each wave also draws a new sample of people, the pooled data form repeated cross-sections rather than a panel, and change over time can be interpreted only as change in the population, never as change within persons. The files are free to download from GESIS with an account, under terms of use that forbid passing the files on, and the [data sources module](companion/data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) describes the procedure step by step.

### 1.3 The question on what the EU means {#sec-item}

The outcome is constructed from a single question that admits several answers. In the questionnaire of spring 2004 the question reads "What does the European Union mean to you personally?", and the interviewer shows a card, reads out the list, records every item that the respondent selects and rotates the order of the list between interviews (variable report for ZA4056, p. 68). Each item is stored as a separate variable, coded 0 for not mentioned and 1 for mentioned. The list comprises fourteen substantive meanings, from 'Peace' and 'Economic prosperity' to 'More crime' and 'Not enough control at external frontiers', besides a spontaneous 'Other' and 'Don't know'. The original author set the 'Euro' aside, because it "shows only low associations with the 13 other items" and "does not have the same meaning among citizens within and outside the Eurozone" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 631, note 1], and assigned the remaining thirteen items to the four dimensions on the evidence of an earlier exploratory analysis and of a confirmatory factor analysis of the pooled data (p. 623).

| Dimension | Items, with the share of respondents who mentioned each |
|:----------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| Cosmopolitan | Peace (28.54%), Democracy (21.86%), Freedom to travel, study and work anywhere in the EU (50.99%), Cultural diversity (22.12%), Stronger say in the world (23.14%) |
| Utilitarian | Economic prosperity (18.66%), Social protection (11.93%) |
| Communitarian | Loss of our cultural identity (12.06%), More crime (17.50%), Not enough control at external borders (16.61%), Unemployment (16.64%) |
| Libertarian | Bureaucracy (21.51%), Waste of money (21.64%) |

: The thirteen items and the four dimensions, with the pooled shares given in the paper (p. 623).

The way in which each dimension is turned into a score bears on everything that follows. In the words of the paper, "the scale is composed of the sum of the mentioned items belonging to the specific framing dimension, divided by the total number of items mentioned by the respondent", and the four scales thus "measure the relative frequency with which the respondent associates each frame to the EU" (p. 623). A respondent who mentions 'Peace', 'Freedom to travel, study and work anywhere in the EU' and 'Bureaucracy' therefore scores 2/3 on the cosmopolitan scale, 1/3 on the libertarian scale and 0 on the other two, and the four scores of anyone who mentions at least one item sum to 1. As each score is a share of what the respondent said rather than a count of meanings, a respondent who adds a negative meaning lowers every positive score without withdrawing any positive item. Pooled over all respondents, the means are 0.534 for the cosmopolitan scale, 0.105 for the utilitarian, 0.208 for the communitarian and 0.153 for the libertarian (Table 1, p. 625), and the [measurement module](companion/measurement.qmd) examines how well the thirteen items support the four dimensions.

### 1.4 The macro indicators {#sec-macro}

The measures of economic conditions are taken from official statistics rather than from the survey, and in the words of the paper the gravity of the crisis "is measured with an indicator of change in the economic performance and an indicator of (absolute) involvement in the economic process, namely the annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth and unemployment rates (Eurostat, 2014)" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 625]. The reference list dates the download to 26 July 2014 but does not name the Eurostat tables (p. 632). The second model presented in the paper adds the annual fiscal transfer of each country to the EU budget, a dummy variable for the countries that received financial stability support, and the average position and salience of European integration among national parties, taken from the Chapel Hill expert surveys conducted in 2002, 2006 and 2010 and weighted by vote shares (p. 625). "All continuous variables are centred on their grand mean" (p. 625), which in the original author's code places the centre of unemployment at 8.76%, of growth at 1.41% and of age at 48 years. The file of macro indicators merged by the code on country and wave was not among the materials supplied by the original author, and the course panel relies instead on the World Bank series of the same two indicators, as described in the [data sources module](companion/data-sources.qmd#sec-worldbank).

### 1.5 Selections made by the original author {#sec-selection}

The original author supplied to SCORE, on request, the two Stata do-files that built and analysed the data, `eb_all.do` and `eb_ml_ESR.do`, which, read beside the paper, show which selections were made and at which stage. The paper states that "The analysis is based on the pooled data of 16 EB waves that took place at least once a year between March 2004 and May 2013 (EB 61.0, 62.0, 63.4, 64.2, 65.2, 67.2, 69.2, 10.1, 72.4, 73.4, 74.2, 75.3, 76.3, 77.3, 78.1, 79.3)", and gives as its reason that "An identical, detailed set of questions on EU framing was asked in these waves" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 622]. 'EB 10.1' is a misprint for EB 70.1, the wave read by the code, and the misprint recurs in the source note of Table 3 (p. 627). The code also reads more than the paper reports, appending eighteen files to a master file of EB 79.3, nineteen waves from 2002 to 2013 in all, of which every model then excludes three, EB 57.1 (2002), EB 59.1 (2003) and EB 71.3 (2009). The paper gives no reason for these exclusions, or for ending the series in May 2013, but the code suggests one for the exclusions, since 'Democracy' has no source variable in the two earliest waves and 'Loss of our cultural identity' none in EB 71.3, leaving 2004 as the first year with the full list in the waves held by the original author.

The sixteen waves, with their GESIS study numbers, versions, fieldwork periods and respondent counts, are listed in the [module on data sources](companion/data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis), and the respondent file built by the course from the same releases ([codebook](data/eb_respondents_codebook.md)) contains 416,698 respondents in all. The file names in the original author's code do not match the names of the current releases, and it was on this mismatch that the push-button reproduction described in section 2.1 also failed.

The paper covers "citizens from the 27 EU member states" (p. 620), and the code assigns the twenty-seven country codes after merging the samples for eastern and western Germany and for Great Britain and Northern Ireland. As the wave of spring 2004 covers only the fifteen states of the time, and the original author did not add the Candidate Countries Eurobarometer that interviewed the then candidate countries in the same weeks (GESIS study ZA4246), the ten states that joined in May 2004 enter the data from autumn 2004. Bulgaria and Romania enter in every wave that sampled the two countries, before and after their accession to the EU in 2007, while Croatia does not appear at all.

Two further questions asked in the same waves, on whether the membership of the country is a good thing and on whether the country has benefited from membership, were used by the original author only to show that the four scales align with support for the EU and with opposition to it (Table 1, p. 625). Squared terms of growth and unemployment were tested and are reported only where such a term reached significance (p. 628), and a comment in the code records that neither did so for the cosmopolitan scale.

Three further decisions are visible only in the code. Since each scale divides by the number of items mentioned, a respondent who mentions none of the thirteen has a denominator of zero, for which Stata returns a missing value, and the respondent thus leaves the analysis without the paper saying so. In the facilitator's re-implementation, the number of respondents in the sixteen waves who named at least one item is exactly 390,373, the level-1 sample reported in the paper (p. 623), while the note to Table 3 gives N = 335,566 (p. 627), a difference most probably attributable to missing values on the model variables. The second decision is that no model uses a weight, and the third lies in the coding of education, which the paper describes as the age at which a respondent left full-time education, grouped into three bands (up to 15, 16 to 19, 20 or older; p. 625), but which in the code assigns to respondents who are still studying a value equal to their current age and retains respondents with no full-time education in the lowest band in two waves, EB 62.0 and EB 79.3, while setting such respondents to missing in the other fourteen.

The course panel scores respondents who mention nothing as 0 on every scale, following the convention of the specification reproduced in the course, and the [specification menu](menu.qmd) offers the rule applied by the original author as an alternative. What each rule assumes about the people who stayed silent is examined in the section [Respondents who mention nothing](companion/measurement.qmd#sec-noop) of the module on scale construction.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Paper and code

A reading of the paper beside the two do-files brings to light three further discrepancies, each of which a reproduction has to resolve one way or the other.

- The text describes level 2 of the model as "16 EB waves" (p. 623), while the code nests country-wave cells within countries.
- The sex variable is initialised as male and replaced where the source variable equals 2, which means that a missing value would be counted as male, although whether any such cases exist was not checked.
- The sentence in which the results are read against H1 begins "This second model" (p. 628), although the passage preceding it describes the first model of Table 3.
:::

### 1.6 The model and the focal estimate {#sec-model}

The original author fitted a multilevel linear model "to take the structure of this repeated cross-sectional sampling design into account: citizens (Level 1; N: 390,373) are sampled within 16 EB waves (Level 2) that repeatedly took place within the 27 EU countries (Level 3)" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. In the code, the second level is the country-wave, the cell comprising all respondents interviewed in one country in one wave, and the model thus nests respondents in country-waves and country-waves in countries, with random intercepts for both. The economic indicators "vary over time and across countries and are, therefore, included as fixed effects at Level 2" (p. 625), where 'fixed effects' carries its multilevel meaning, coefficients that take the same value in every country rather than varying at random between countries, as distinct from the econometric meaning, adopted in several of the reanalyses, of a separate intercept for each country. Model 1 of Table 3 includes sex, age, education in three bands, occupation in eight groups, type of community, GDP growth, unemployment, and the interactions of each economic indicator with education. The line of the do-file that fits this model for the cosmopolitan scale reads as follows.

```         
mixed cos female mage i.edu3 b4.ses b3.urban  mgrowth munemp  c.mgrowth##edu3 c.munemp##edu3|| cty:   || eb_ctr:  if eb!=203 & eb!=303 &eb!=906 , covariance(unstructured)
```

The focal estimate is the coefficient of unemployment in the cosmopolitan column of Model 1, −0.00340 with t = −4.03 (Table 3, pp. 626–627). A rise of one percentage point in the national unemployment rate is associated with a cosmopolitan share lower by 0.0034, about a third of a percentage point of the meanings mentioned by respondents, against a pooled mean of 0.534. Because the continuous variables are centred and the model includes the interactions with education, the coefficient corresponds to the slope for respondents in the low-education band at average growth rather than to an average over all respondents, and adding the interaction terms printed in Table 3 yields slopes of −0.00478 for the middle band and −0.00646 for the high band. Model 2, which adds the variables on EU policies and party positions, puts the same coefficient at −0.00138 with t = −1.54 (p. 627), which means that the significant association reported in the claim derives from Model 1. The original author read the results as support for the part of H1 that concerns direction, concluding that "poor economic performances significantly increase the negative and significantly decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. However, the materialist EU-framing dimensions are not more affected by the national economic performances" (p. 628).

## 2. SCORE {#sec-score}

### 2.1 Reproduction, robustness and replication {#sec-repetition}

SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, was a programme [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen] that subjected the claims of papers published in social and behavioural science journals to three kinds of repetition – reproduction, robustness check and replication – each of which is defined in the [glossary](resources.qmd#glossary). The papers were drawn as "a stratified random sample of 600 articles" from about 30,000 published in 62 journals between 2009 and 2018 [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods], and the three kinds of study were reported together in *Nature* in April 2026 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial].

The paper went through all three kinds of study. In the SCORE reproducibility study, a push-button reproduction run with the original author's code failed before producing any number, because "the authors used file names that did not correspond with the names of the files available for download. Additionally 16 datasets are listed on the website as being used but the code references 18 files", in the words of the report on the attempt, while a second reproduction, from the source data, was recorded as 'not reproduced'. The five reanalyses produced by the robustness study are the subject of section 3. The replication of the claim in the SCORE replicability study, on fourteen Standard Eurobarometer waves fielded between 2013 and 2019, found a positive coefficient for unemployment, opposite in sign to the claim and not significant, and SCORE judged the replication not successful. All of these materials are public on the Open Science Framework (OSF), and @fig-osf shows how the materials are organised there.

::: column-page
![The SCORE dossier on the paper, as it is organised on the OSF. Each panel holds the OSF nodes of one kind of study, and in the full-size diagram every node links to its OSF page.](assets/diagrams/score-teney-osf.svg){#fig-osf fig-alt="Diagram of the SCORE dossier on the OSF in four panels: the original materials, the two reproductions, the five reanalyses of the robustness study with the fork kept by analyst C6HJR, and the replication on later waves with its preregistration and both reports."}
:::

The diagram can be [opened at full size](assets/diagrams/score-teney-osf.svg), in which form its links are active, and the [repositories module](companion/repositories.qmd#sec-trail-europeanisation) uses the same tree to show how such a record is kept and what it allows a reader to establish without writing to anyone.

### 2.2 How the robustness study worked {#sec-robustness}

The design of the robustness study is described on the [SCORE page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/score.html#sec-robustness) of the AR4DS site: 100 claims, each given to several independent analysts, and two tasks, a free analysis ending in a single conclusion in Task 1 and, in Task 2, one statistical result produced under an instruction from the lead team. Each claim had been extracted from the abstract of its paper in an earlier phase of SCORE as a 'single trace', one claim that "ideally corresponded to one statistically significant inferential test result" (preregistration of the robustness study, [osf.io/4ev9t](https://osf.io/4ev9t), p. 5). The lead team then checked that each extraction was understandable, contained only one claim, indicated the direction of the effect and corresponded to a test reported in the paper, replacing any wording judged ambiguous or rhetorical with an ellipsis (p. 5). The claim taken from this paper reached the analysts as "... poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing. (p. 619.)", a trimmed version of the sentence from the abstract quoted in section 1.1. As the Eurobarometer files may not be passed on, no dataset accompanied this paper, and every analyst therefore rebuilt the data from the GESIS archive.

The instructions for Task 2 were intended to make each result comparable with one result of the original paper while leaving the analysis to the analyst. The preregistration required that the instructions "remain circumstantial (e.g., data selection, exclusions) and never give direct instructions to the choice of statistical approach or full specification of the model" (p. 6), and the published Methods describe such instructions as "circumstantial (for example, data selection, exclusions and choice of measurement)" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. The instruction for this claim, quoted below, chooses both the outcome and the predictor, which amounts to a choice of measurement, and removes the variables of Model 2, thereby restricting the specification without writing it out.

### 2.3 The Task 2 instruction {#sec-instruction}

The instruction is quoted here in the form in which the analysts received it.

> **Claim:**
>
> **"... poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing"** (p. 619)
>
> The original paper's results that refer to Task 2 were shown in their 'Model 1 – Cosmopolitan' column in Table 3, 'Unempl. rate' independent variable: estimate = -0.00340; t statistic = -4.03; P \< 0.001
>
> **Task 2:**
>
> - produce a single, main result in terms of statistical families of z-, t-, F-, or $\chi^2$ tests (or their alternative or non-parametric versions).
> - disregard contextual variables related to the EU policies and party EU salience and party EU positions indexes in your analysis.
> - use the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** in your analysis.
> - use the **unemployment rate** as the measure for poor economic performance in your analysis.

Read literally, the second bullet removes the variables of Model 2 and leaves the rest of Model 1, with its individual controls, GDP growth and the interactions with education, to the judgement of the analyst. Four of the five analysts, however, fitted unemployment as the only predictor, and in practice the instruction thus appears to have narrowed the analyses further than its literal reading required.

## 3. The five reanalysts {#sec-reanalysts}

The five analysts were assigned identifier codes by the robustness study, and in this course we refer to each analyst by that code. Three described their discipline as sociology and two as psychology, while three worked in R and two in Stata, and all five concluded in Task 1 that the data showed evidence for the claim. What each analyst did in Task 2 is summarised in @tbl-overview, and the sections that follow present the five in the order in which the analysts submitted, quoting the reports filed by the analysts with the robustness study and made public in its data.

::: column-body-outset
| Analyst | Data in Task 2 | Outcome | Unemployment series | Model | Recorded result |
|:-----------|:-----------|:-----------|:------------|:-----------|:-----------|
| KQXUE | 270 country-years | share of mentions | Eurostat, as a share of the population aged 20–64 | an intercept for each country | t = −7.17, 242 df |
| C6HJR | 270 country-years | share of mentions | World Bank | an intercept for each country and each year | t = −3.80, 233 df |
| KEVF1 | 209,826 respondents | count of the five items | Eurostat `tipsun20` | random intercepts for years within countries | t = −5.90, 135.6 df |
| PRL47 | 394,575 respondents | share of mentions, without the respondents who mentioned nothing | Eurostat, quarterly, ages 25–64 | three levels, random slopes, individual and national controls | z = −3.59 |
| 018OL | 420 country-wave cells | mean of the five items, rescaled to 0–1 | Eurostat, ages 15–74 | random intercepts for country, year and wave | t = −1.21, 396.9 df |

: The five reanalyses in Task 2, with the result as recorded in the robustness study. {#tbl-overview}
:::

### 3.1 KQXUE {#sec-kqxue}

KQXUE, an assistant professor of sociology with fifteen years of experience in data analysis, submitted first, in May 2022, answering both tasks with written reports uploaded to the OSF in place of the free-text fields of the submission form ("Please see the document writeup.pdf that I uploaded"). The analyst's Stata code reads the respondents of each wave from the GESIS files, drops the euro item, builds the scales as shares of mentions, as the paper does, and collapses the pooled waves to means for each country and year before merging these means with Eurostat series of GDP growth and unemployment. In Task 1 the analyst fitted, for the cosmopolitan and utilitarian scales and with the two economic indicators separately and together, both models with a separate intercept for each country, which compare each country only with itself over time, and models of the differences between countries. For Task 2 the model was a regression of the cosmopolitan share on unemployment with an intercept for each country (`xtreg cosmo unemployment, fe`). The first Task 2 entry reported t = −0.007, with the degrees of freedom entered as "Errr no idea", and the second, in September 2022, reported t = −7.169 on 242 degrees of freedom, accompanied by the remark that "It was quite a lot as the paper wasn't particularly clear about the data it used and I needed to check a few things" and the conclusion that "A higher unemployment rate is associated with weaker support for a cosmopolitan EU framing".

### 3.2 C6HJR {#sec-c6hjr}

C6HJR, the facilitator of this course, submitted in November 2022, having rebuilt the data from GESIS and the World Bank because "the code provided by the authors were not really useful for reconstructing the original datasets". The main choice of design is described in the Task 1 report: "I reduced the dataset from one with three levels (individual respondents, countries and years) to one containing country-year averages for the measurements of interest; this resulted in a balanced dataset of 270 country-year data points (10 years across 27 EU countries)." In Task 1 a single positive scale combined all seven positive items, and a model of the two-way kind described below, with GDP growth and unemployment as predictors, found that "When accounting for both GDP growth and unemployment rate, an increase in unemployment is associated with a small reduction in positive EU framing". For Task 2 the outcome became the cosmopolitan share and GDP growth was dropped, and the report explains why the analysis remains at the level of the country-year: "Since the predictor was a contextual variable measured at country-year level, I collapsed the individual-level data to obtain a balanced panel dataset of 270 country-year cases (27 EU countries across 10 years). To account for country and year effects, I fit a two-way fixed effects panel model using the `plm` package (version 2.6.2) in `R`." The two-way model has a separate intercept for each country and for each year, which means that each country is compared with itself over time after the change shared by all countries in a given year has been removed. The analyst reported t = −3.853 on 233 degrees of freedom, and the robustness study recorded t = −3.804 (section 3.7).

### 3.3 KEVF1 {#sec-kevf1}

KEVF1, a professor of psychology with twenty years of experience in data analysis, worked in R and retained the respondents as the unit of analysis. In Task 1 the analyst summed the seven positive items and the six negative ones into two scores and regressed each score on GDP growth in mixed models in which "data was nested within country and year", concluding that "A decline in GDP growth decreases the positive attitude towards the European Union and increases the negative attitude towards the European Union". For Task 2 the outcome was the sum of the five cosmopolitan items, a count from 0 to 5, and the predictor an unemployment series from Eurostat, with a consequence that the report states openly: "Note that unemployment rate was not available for the UK, and only from 2009 for the remaining countries. That left 209,826 observations." The model has random intercepts for countries and for years within countries, and the report gives its result as "beta = -.0295, t(135.606) = -5.899, p \< .001". The degrees of freedom come from the Satterthwaite approximation, computed by the lmerTest package as an estimate of how much independent information a mixed model holds about each coefficient, and as unemployment takes one value per country-year, the approximation counts cells rather than respondents. The statistic was recorded on the form as +5.899, and the lead team of the robustness study changed its sign to agree with the text.

### 3.4 PRL47 {#sec-prl47}

PRL47, a postdoctoral researcher in sociology, spent 60 hours on the two tasks, the most of the five, and built the design closest to that of the original study. The Task 1 report reconstructs the wave list with care, adding the Candidate Countries Eurobarometer of spring 2004 on the reasoning that the article uses data from the candidate countries for that year, and reading 'EB 10.1' as EB 70.1, since "the EB 10 was fielded in 1978". Task 1 used GDP per capita and quarterly growth as predictors, with a dummy variable for the debt crisis, in three-level models in which "the individuals (Level 1) are nested in country-waves (Level 2) which are nested in countries (Level 3)", and the report closes with a caution: "As the ICCs show, there is very little variance on country or country-wave level and some of the significant relationships found in the three-level-models might simply be a result of the large sample." In Task 2 the cosmopolitan share was built in two versions, one in which "respondents who did not mention any of the aspects are coded '0'" and one in which "they are excluded (coded as missing)", while the predictor was the quarterly unemployment rate of people aged 25 to 64, chosen "because in most European countries most people will have finished their education" by that age. The reported model, the version without the silent respondents, added individual controls, national prosperity, growth, the crisis dummy and the change in unemployment, and allowed the slopes of the individual variables to vary between countries. Stata reported the result of that model as z = −3.594 for 394,575 respondents and, as its `mixed` command does for any such model, without degrees of freedom.

### 3.5 018OL {#sec-018ol}

018OL, a postdoctoral researcher in psychology who analyses data daily, wrote both tasks as R Markdown documents. In Task 1 the outcome was the proportion of the seven positive items mentioned by a respondent, computed "by summing the positive dimensions checked and dividing them by the number of possible positive dimensions", averaged by year, country and wave, and the predictor was GDP per capita. A mixed model with "the random intercepts of year, country and eurobarometer wave" gave "estimate = 0.32 \[CI 0.10 - 0.54\], p = 0.005". In Task 2 the outcome became the mean of the five cosmopolitan items, the predictor the annual unemployment rate of people aged 15 to 74 from Eurostat, and the data 420 cells of one country in one wave, whose means, according to the report, were log-transformed before the same kind of model was fitted, although the deposited code rescales the means to run from 0 to 1 and takes no logarithm. The result was t = −1.206 on 396.9 degrees of freedom (p = 0.228), and the analyst concluded that "Economic performance as measured in unemployment rate did not predict positive non-materialist form of EU framing", while ticking, for a negative estimate, the box for a result "Opposite as claimed by the original study".

### 3.6 Assessment {#sec-assessment}

Three differences separate the five analyses before any question of the model arises. The first is the unit of analysis, with two analysts working on 270 country-years, one on 420 country-wave cells and two on several hundred thousand respondents. Since the predictor takes one value per country and year, or per country and quarter in the case of PRL47, the evidence on its slope lies in a few hundred pairings of a national unemployment rate with a national level of framing, whatever the number of rows, and for the respondent-level models the degrees of freedom therefore matter more than the sample sizes.

The second difference lies in the construction of the outcome, for which three analysts used the share of mentions, as the paper does, KEVF1 the count of the five cosmopolitan items and 018OL the mean of those items, which is the same count divided by five. A share and a count are different variables, and across the country-years of the course panel the two constructions of the cosmopolitan outcome correlate at only 0.44, the count tracking how much respondents say about the EU at all, since it correlates at 0.85 with the mean number of items mentioned, where the share correlates at −0.07. The count therefore arguably answers a neighbouring question, whether people name more or fewer positive things, rather than the claim as the paper measured it.

The third difference concerns the treatment of the respondents who mention nothing, about 6.3% of those interviewed in the sixteen waves. The original author's code and that of KQXUE drop these respondents by dividing by zero, C6HJR scored them 0, PRL47 ran both versions and reported the one without them, and KEVF1 and 018OL retain them with a score of 0 by construction, since a count or a mean needs no denominator of mentions.

The two fixed-effects analyses, those of KQXUE and C6HJR with an intercept for each country, share a further problem, which concerns the standard errors rather than the estimates. Both analysts used conventional errors, which treat the 270 country-years as 270 independent pieces of evidence, although on the course panel the residuals of the C6HJR specification correlate at 0.53 from one year to the next within a country, and the variation from which the slope is identified is concentrated in a few countries, with Greece contributing 17.5% of the variation in unemployment that remains once country and year effects are removed, Spain 15.9% and Poland 10.6%. The course therefore classes every result with errors clustered by country under the CR2 correction [@BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard], tested on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom [@PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust], as explained in the [module on panel data](companion/panel-data.qmd#sec-inference).

Under every rule the estimate and the partial correlation remain unchanged, and only the verdict on significance differs. The CR2 correction allows for the unequal influence of the countries on the fit, and its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom indicate that the 27 countries carry about as much information as ten would. Under the rule adopted by the course, the reproduced result falls just short of significance at the 5% level (p = 0.0504 on 9.8 degrees of freedom), although it would pass under CR1 (p = 0.029), while the design chosen by KQXUE, fitted on the same panel, remains significant under every correction (CR1 p = 0.001, CR2 p = 0.007 on 8.5 degrees of freedom).

**KQXUE** worked at the level of the predictor and built the outcome as the paper did, and the course reproduces the recorded result exactly (t = −7.169) on a panel rebuilt from the GESIS waves by following the deposited code, a reproduction offered in Task 3 of the browser lab. The design has an intercept for each country but none for each year, and the comparison within each country therefore includes the changes that all of Europe went through in a given year. On the course panel, year effects absorb 29% of the variation of unemployment within countries, and without year effects the slope is larger (−0.00564 against −0.00347 for the two-way design) and open to confounding by any Europe-wide shift in framing that coincided with the crisis. Unemployment entered as a share of the whole population aged 20–64 rather than of the labour force, a different quantity, averaging 6.3% across the panel where the rate in the labour force averages 8.7%, and the Turkish Cypriot sample was merged into Cyprus, a step not taken in the paper.

**C6HJR** also worked at the level of the predictor, with a two-way design that removes both the stable differences between countries and the changes common to Europe in each year, leaving the comparison within countries over time with which the claim is concerned. The analyst's pipeline is public and reproduces the recorded value exactly from the GESIS files. The standard errors are conventional, with the problem described above, and the analysis departs from the paper in three ways: World Bank series in place of Eurostat and, in Task 1, one positive scale in place of the two positive dimensions, both stated in the reports, and respondents who mention nothing scored 0 rather than dropped, which the reports do not mention. The build first submitted by the analyst also read one wave twice, a slip corrected before the robustness study recorded the value (section 3.7).

**KEVF1** retained the respondents but declared their grouping in countries and years, and the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of the model (135.6) count cells rather than respondents. A refit of the design on the rebuilt respondent file yields r = −0.492 when converted on its own Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, against −0.499 for the same design fitted on the cell means, a comparison which indicates that the recorded value is a cell-level quantity and that the small gap to the record arises from the data rather than from the conversion. The design has three weaknesses for this claim, the first being that the outcome is a count rather than a share. Second, the series `tipsun20` has no row for the United Kingdom and nothing before 2009 except for France, and the analysis thus rests on 135 cells, mostly from the crisis years, losing the comparison with the years before the crisis without saying so. The third weakness is that the t of the model rests on errors which treat the years of a country as independent once the country intercept is removed, and on the same cells the t of a model with an intercept for each country falls from −5.27 to −3.13 when its errors are clustered by country, while a two-way model yields a weaker association (r = −0.378).

**PRL47** built the design closest to the original, with respondents in country-periods in countries, individual controls, the share of mentions and both treatments of the silent respondents, and documented a search over unemployment measures with candid cautions about sample size. The reported model, however, departs from Model 1 in ways that change what it estimates, adding national controls absent from Model 1, among them a crisis dummy that, in the words of the analyst, "weakens the relationship between unemployment rates and cosmopolitan EU-framing, indicating that part of the negative relationship is due to the crisis", and allowing the individual slopes to vary between countries. It also adds the Candidate Countries wave, in which non-response to the items was recoded as 'not mentioned', and interpolates the missing quarters of unemployment. The facilitator's re-implementation does not recover the result (z = −8.38 against −3.59), and which of these departures explains the gap is not known.

**018OL** wrote a literate pipeline with cached intermediate data and found the items by their labels, a method that survives the renumbering of variables between waves, and the random intercepts for country, year and wave arguably describe the structure of the data more fully than most of the other designs. The outcome, however, is a mean of five items rather than a share, which according to the report was log-transformed and which the code rescales to run from 0 to 1. Because the code dates the wave EB 79.3, fielded in 2013, to 2012, the 420 country-wave cells share the annual unemployment rates of 27 countries in nine years, with cells of the same country-year carrying the same value of the predictor, and the 396.9 degrees of freedom thus most probably overstate the number of independent comparisons. Without an intercept for each country, stable national differences enter the slope to the extent that the random intercepts do not absorb these differences. The box ticked for the direction of the result marked a negative estimate as opposite to the claim, and the robustness study carried that marking into the effect size, as section 4 shows. A rebuild that dates every wave by its fieldwork does not recover the result (t = −1.61 against −1.21), while one that keeps the analyst's dating reproduces it exactly, and Task 3 of the browser lab offers this reproduction. The items found by their labels and by their positions are the same in all sixteen files.

### 3.7 Reanalyst coding errors {#sec-slips}

Two of the five pipelines read the wrong set of waves. In the build submitted by C6HJR, the preparation script read the file of EB 70.1 (ZA4819) twice, correctly for 2008 and again for 2009 in place of EB 72.4 (ZA4994), which it never read, with the result that the 2009 cells held respondents of 2008 under a new label. The submitted result was t = −3.853 and the corrected one t = −3.804, the two builds differing only in 2009 and leading to the same conclusion. The analyst found the error and annotated the script with the comment `# APRIL 2025 - Mistake in dataset here; the dataset associated with "eb724" should be "ZA4994_v3-0-0.dta"`. The fork maintained by the analyst on the OSF ([osf.io/6zqct](https://osf.io/6zqct/)) holds both versions, while the archival record kept by the robustness study ([osf.io/8rtwe](https://osf.io/8rtwe/)) contains only the uncorrected folder. The value recorded for this analysis in the robustness study, however, reflects the corrected build.

KQXUE appended the file of EB 62.0, the wave of autumn 2004, twice, in the code of both tasks (lines 441 and 442 of `task2.do`), with the consequence that the autumn wave counts double in the 2004 means of the fifteen older member states, while for the states not sampled by EB 61.0 the duplicated wave is the only one of the year, and the means of those states are unchanged. Refitted with the wave counted once, the model gives t = −7.166 in place of the −7.169 on record, which means that the slip barely moves the estimate.

The code written by 018OL contains a slip of dating rather than of reading, taking the year of each wave from the first four characters of the name given to its file by the analyst, a rule that put EB 79.3, fielded in 2013, in 2012. The cells of that wave therefore take the unemployment of 2012, and the data cover nine years rather than ten. With the wave dated by its fieldwork, the same model gives t = −1.606 in place of the −1.206 on record.

None of the three slips leaves a trace in a table of results, whereas all three become apparent at once in the inputs, where a list of the files read shows the repeated file name, a count of respondents by wave and year shows the duplicate, and a date for each wave shows the wave placed in the wrong year. In the C6HJR build, 2009 holds 26,618 respondents, exactly as many as the EB 70.1 wave of autumn 2008, since that file was read a second time under the label of 2009, whereas a correct build holds the 26,731 respondents of EB 72.4. Three checks written into a pipeline would detect all three errors: an assertion that no input file is read twice, an assertion of one wave per fieldwork period with its date and the expected number of respondents, and a cell-by-cell comparison of two builds that reports every cell that differs.

An AI coding assistant can act as a second reader of the code before a result is submitted, listing the files read against the waves named in the paper, flagging repeated reads and waves appended twice and checking how country codes and missing codes are treated. A reading of this kind finds all three slips from the code and the aggregate outputs alone, without opening any data. The use of such an assistant on the data themselves is forbidden by the terms of use of GESIS, which state that "The use of AI systems for processing the database provided to the user by GESIS is prohibited", as both the [data sources module](companion/data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) and the AR4DS module on [AI assistants](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/ai.html) explain.

## 4. Cross-analyst comparisons {#sec-back}

### 4.1 From test statistics to effect sizes {#sec-conversion}

The five results in @tbl-overview cannot be compared as they stand, since they are coefficients on a share, on a count and on a rescaled mean, tested by t and z statistics on bases ranging from 135.6 degrees of freedom to 394,575 respondents. The robustness study faced the same problem with all 504 reanalyses and chose, in the words of the article, to "transform the reported point estimates into a standard effect-size measure", while acknowledging that "these transformations have limitations and their calculation relies on assumptions that may not hold in all considered analysis settings" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]. Each statistic was first converted into a correlation and then into Cohen's d, the standardised difference adopted as the common scale of the project. For a t statistic the rule is

$$ r = \frac{t}{\sqrt{t^{2} + df}}, $$

which returns the partial correlation between outcome and predictor, net of everything else in the model, provided that the degrees of freedom count the units that carry the evidence. As a z statistic has no degrees of freedom, the code of the robustness study converts it on the sample size N instead, as $r = \tanh\left(|z| / \sqrt{N - 3}\right)$ with the sign of z, a rule that treats every row of the data as an independent unit. In either case the correlation then becomes $d = 2r / \sqrt{1 - r^{2}}$. The sign follows a convention under which "the reanalysis effect sizes are negative only when they indicate an opposite effect compared with the original study" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods], and the direction was read from the box ticked by each analyst rather than from the sign of the estimate.

Every reported statistic also passed through a cleaning step, in which, for this claim, the cleaning sheet queried the degrees of freedom entered by KQXUE as "1; 242" and settled them at 242 after contacting the analyst, removed the description of model parameters that PRL47 had entered in place of degrees of freedom, changed the sign of the statistic reported by KEVF1 to agree with the text of the report, and replaced the t = −3.853 reported by C6HJR with −3.804, the value of the corrected build, without recording a note for these last two changes.

### 4.2 The tolerance region {#sec-tolerance}

The comparison with the original studies was preregistered as a tolerance region, under which a reanalysis counted as different "if its effect size is beyond the +/-0.05 Cohen's d tolerance region of the original result", a rule preferred to tests of difference because "Cohen's ds are independent of sample size" (preregistration, p. 9). This claim never entered that comparison, since no original effect size could be computed for it. The record of the robustness study marks the original effect size as not available, and the original study is one of the five listed at the foot of Figure 2 of the article, for which "we could not determine the original effect size because of missing information" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 137]. The independence from sample size, however, arguably holds only within one design, and it cannot be taken for granted across analyses that count different units for the same predictor, as the five reanalyses of this claim do.

### 4.3 The five results as recorded {#sec-recorded}

The five results as recorded in the robustness study are given in @tbl-recorded. The recorded correlations range from −0.006 to −0.452, a ratio of 79, while the test statistics behind these correlations range from −1.21 to −7.17, a ratio of 5.9, which suggests that most of the additional spread arises from the conversion rather than from the analyses. PRL47 and C6HJR report almost the same statistic (z = −3.59 and t = −3.80), yet their recorded correlations differ 42-fold, because the z was converted on 394,575 respondents and the t on 233 degrees of freedom. The original study has no recorded effect size at all, and its t = −4.03, if converted by the rule for z on the respondent count of Table 3, would give r = −0.007, the same artefact as for PRL47.

The course places each result on the degrees of freedom of its own inference, in keeping with the requirement that the degrees of freedom count the units that carry the evidence. Where an analyst's software counted those units, the recorded value stands, as it does for KQXUE (−0.419) and C6HJR (−0.242) on their residual degrees of freedom and for 018OL (−0.060) and KEVF1 (−0.452) on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which in the case of KEVF1 already count cells rather than respondents (section 3.6). The result of PRL47, reported as a z without degrees of freedom, is converted on the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of a refit of the analyst's design on the rebuilt respondents, a conversion that places the result at −0.176 on 404.5 degrees of freedom. The original study is placed differently, since its published coefficient belongs to a model with interactions between education and the two economic measures and thus corresponds to the slope of unemployment for the low-education band alone. The course places instead a refit of the same design without the interactions, whose slope is the average over the education bands, as in the five reanalyses (b = −0.0060, t = −8.39 on 403.9 Satterthwaite degrees of freedom), and this refit places the original study at −0.385. As both refits approximate the published designs rather than reproducing them, the two placements are best read as the order of magnitude that each result takes when its own design sets the units, and the [data codebook](data/reference_marks_codebook.md) records what each refit leaves out.

A common denominator offers a second reading of the record, applying to every statistic the 233 degrees of freedom of the two-way design on the 270 country-years. Such a denominator treats each result as if it came from that design, which is why the course uses it only as a teaching device, but it shows how much of the recorded spread arose from the conversion, and the task in section 4.6 asks the class to carry out this conversion.

### 4.4 Findings of the Nature article {#sec-findings}

What the article found about the numbers and conclusions of the 504 reanalyses, and about how observational studies such as this one fared against experiments, is presented on the AR4DS page on [the robustness article](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/robustness-article.html#sec-findings) [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. Among the 100 claims, this claim counts among those that were robust in their conclusions, since all five reanalysts reached the conclusion of the original study in Task 1, while its Task 2 estimates spread by a factor of 79 in r, include one non-significant result and enter no comparison with an original effect size. The article names five sources of variability between analysts – the ambiguity of the research question, alternative operationalisations of concepts, alternative preprocessing of the data, alternative models and methods, and undiscovered errors (Fig. 1, p. 136) – and this one case study contains an instance of each. The claim names 'poor economic performances' and two positive dimensions, the outcome was built in three ways, the wave lists were read differently and the silent respondents treated in three ways, five different estimators were used, and two pipelines duplicated a wave. The authors of the article themselves "caution against using blanket rules in aggregating or interpreting results across different analytical approaches within the same investigation" (p. 141).

### 4.5 Reading the article {#sec-reading}

This case study points to three things to look for in a converted effect size, while the general advice on reading such an effect size is given on the AR4DS page on [the robustness article](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/robustness-article.html#sec-reading).

- **The units in the formula.** A conversion may use the residual degrees of freedom of a model, a Satterthwaite approximation, or a respondent count standing in for degrees of freedom never reported by the software, and the same z converts to −0.006 or to about −0.18 depending on that choice.
- **The sign.** The sign was taken from the box ticked by each analyst rather than from the estimate, and it was in this way that a negative estimate by 018OL entered the record as an effect in the opposite direction, d = −0.121.
- **The clustered test.** Converting the CR2 t of C6HJR (−2.23 on 9.8 degrees of freedom) would give r = −0.581 for an unchanged estimate, which is why the course retains the correlation of the conventional fit and uses the clustered test only for the verdict on significance.

### 4.6 Recomputing the correlations {#sec-task}

The conversion takes one line of R code. Download [`analysts5.csv`](data/analysts5.csv), which holds the five recorded rows, into the `data` folder of your workspace, and run the following in your IDE.

``` r
analysts <- readr::read_csv("data/analysts5.csv")
analysts |> dplyr::mutate(r_233 = statistic / sqrt(statistic^2 + 233))
```

The second line places every statistic on the 233 degrees of freedom of the two-way design. Compare the new column `r_233` with the recorded `r`, sort the five both ways and note which analysts change places. Then repeat the conversion with each statistic on its own degrees of freedom, the column `df1`, and decide what to do with the row that has none.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

On 233 degrees of freedom the order becomes KQXUE, KEVF1, C6HJR, PRL47 and 018OL, and the ratio between the largest and the smallest of the five correlations falls from 79 to 5.4. PRL47 moves from last place to fourth, beside C6HJR, which is where its test statistic always put it, and KEVF1 drops to second place, because the 135.6 Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of its model give a larger correlation than the same t earns on 233. On its own degrees of freedom, PRL47 needs a value from outside the file: the course takes the 404.5 Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of a refit of its design. The row of the original study gives the refit of its design without the education interactions, with its own statistic and degrees of freedom.
